proposals.relationship: James names Ibn Khaldun as a particular resource for teaching the philosophy of history as part of the humanities.
proposals.evidence_note: Own November 1977 interview excerpt, published and edited by interviewer Alan Warhaftig in 2023, answer to “What are you teaching?”, says he devoted one or two sessions to Ibn Khaldun and praises his account of what history means. This records a discrete teaching resource, not demonstrated early formation, adoption of a whole historical system or a newly read original treatise. James identifies no title in this answer, so none is supplied. The separate October 1976 Minty Alley conversation is not assigned the 1977 date.
primary_locators: 2023 original LARB publication, first interview excerpt (12–13 November 1977), answer to “What are you teaching?”

proposals.relationship: Douglas identifies James’s intensive reading of Marx, alongside Trotsky and political encounters in Nelson, as part of his turn toward revolutionary historical writing.
proposals.evidence_note: Named substantive scholar Rachel Douglas, article 284, connects James’s reading of Marx and Trotsky in England with the research that produced the 1936 play and 1938 history, retaining Harry Spencer’s practical and political role. Her note 17 cites James’s Beyond a Boundary, 151; that original passage is not newly read here. This is explicit scholarly mediation, not a verified exact first-reading date or Marx as sole source. Existing historical-materialism group edge 264 remains distinct; no identity is collapsed between that tradition and the person Karl Marx.
primary_locators: Douglas, Atlantic Studies 19:2 (2022), 283–284, Nelson/Spencer discussion and note 17 at 297

proposals.relationship: Douglas reads James’s active restoration of enslaved people’s historical agency through Trouillot’s account of how historical silences are produced.
proposals.evidence_note: Douglas 282–283 and notes 11–13 explicitly builds on Trouillot’s active, transitive account of silencing to interpret James’s history and drama as a reverse process of unsilencing. This is Douglas’s retrospective methodological comparison, not James borrowing a 1995 book after his death, proof that Trouillot directly read James, identical theories or an assertion that all archival gaps can be filled. Fischer and Buck-Morss are separately credited in Douglas’s genealogy. Neither Trouillot’s original nor complete James books newly read.
primary_locators: Douglas (2022), “Caribbean quarrels and unsilencing,” 282–283, paragraph beginning “From the beginning” and next paragraph; notes 11–13 at 297
